lessons.title: Introduction
body: An Android app is not one long-running program. The system starts and stops its **components** (Activities, Services, BroadcastReceivers and ContentProviders) whenever it needs to, and it can kill your whole process at any time to free memory.
Interviewers test whether you design for this: state that survives rotation and process death, work that keeps going when the screen goes away, and no leaks of a dead `Context`.
points: The four app components and what each is for
The system, not you, owns the lifecycle
Process death is normal, not an edge case
lessons.tip: When asked "what happens when the user rotates the phone?", answer in three parts: the Activity is destroyed and recreated, ViewModel survives, and savedInstanceState covers process death.

code.title: The four components in the manifest
code.src:
<application android:name=".App">
    <activity android:name=".MainActivity" android:exported="true">
        <intent-filter>
            <action android:name="android.intent.action.MAIN" />
            <category android:name="android.intent.category.LAUNCHER" />
        </intent-filter>
    </activity>
    <service android:name=".PlayerService" android:foregroundServiceType="mediaPlayback" />
    <receiver android:name=".BootReceiver" android:exported="false" />
    <provider android:name=".FilesProvider" android:authorities="io.app.files" />
</application>

lessons.title: Activity lifecycle
body: An Activity moves through `onCreate` → `onStart` → `onResume` when it comes to the front, and `onPause` → `onStop` → `onDestroy` as it leaves. **Started** means visible, **resumed** means it has focus and takes input.

A configuration change (rotation, dark mode, language) destroys and recreates the Activity. Pressing Home only stops it. The process can then be killed while stopped, and the user returns to a fresh Activity that receives the saved `Bundle`.
points: onCreate: inflate UI, restore state, set up observers
onStart/onStop: visible or not; start and stop UI work here
onResume/onPause: foreground focus; keep it fast
isChangingConfigurations tells rotation apart from finishing
onSaveInstanceState runs before the Activity may be killed
lessons.tip: Know the order when Activity A starts Activity B: A.onPause → B.onCreate → B.onStart → B.onResume → A.onStop. It is a very common trick question.

code.title: Lifecycle-aware collection instead of manual start and stop

lessons.title: Fragments and their two lifecycles
body: A Fragment has its own lifecycle **and** a separate view lifecycle. On the back stack, the Fragment object stays alive while its view is destroyed (`onDestroyView`) and later recreated.
That is why you observe with `viewLifecycleOwner` and clear the view binding in `onDestroyView`. Otherwise you leak a whole view tree, or receive duplicate observers each time the view comes back.
points: Communicate through a shared ViewModel or the Fragment Result API, not direct references
FragmentManager back stack and commit vs commitNow
lessons.tip: If an interviewer asks about a memory leak in a Fragment, the binding held past onDestroyView is the first thing to mention.

code.title: Safe view binding in a Fragment

lessons.title: Intents, tasks and launch modes
body: An **explicit** Intent names the component to start; an **implicit** Intent describes an action (`ACTION_VIEW`, `ACTION_SEND`) and the system finds an app that matches an intent filter. Since Android 12, any component with an intent filter must declare `android:exported`.

Activities live in **tasks** (back stacks). Launch modes and flags such as `singleTop`, `singleTask` and `FLAG_ACTIVITY_CLEAR_TOP` control whether a new instance is created or an existing one receives `onNewIntent`.
points: PendingIntent lets another app (e.g. notifications) start your component; choose FLAG_IMMUTABLE by default
lessons.tip: Mention that PendingIntents should be FLAG_IMMUTABLE unless something must fill in extras; it is a security question disguised as an API question.

code.title: Handling a deep link that may arrive twice

lessons.title: Services, background work and process death
body: A **foreground service** shows a notification and is for work the user is aware of right now: music, navigation, an active call. Modern Android heavily restricts background services, so deferrable work belongs in **WorkManager**, which survives reboots and respects battery constraints.

For UI state, use **ViewModel** for rotation and **SavedStateHandle** (backed by the saved Bundle) for process death. Keep only small, essential state there, such as IDs and scroll position, not whole lists.
points: Foreground service vs WorkManager vs coroutine in a ViewModel
Process death: how to test it ("Don't keep activities", or adb shell am kill)
lessons.tip: Ask yourself "what if the process dies here?" out loud during design questions. It signals real production experience.

code.title: Surviving process death with SavedStateHandle

lessons.title: Introduction
body: Kotlin interviews rarely ask you to recite syntax. They check whether you use the type system to make bugs impossible: nullability, immutable data, exhaustive `when`, and small functions that compose.
Expect questions that compare features (`val` vs `const`, `data` vs regular class, `let` vs `apply`) and "what does this compile to" questions about `inline`, `object` and extension functions.
lessons.tip: Write answers in idiomatic Kotlin even on a whiteboard: expression bodies, immutable vals and the elvis operator read as fluency.

code.title: Idiomatic Kotlin in a few lines

lessons.title: Null safety
body: Every type is either nullable (`String?`) or not (`String`), and the compiler forces you to handle null before use. Use `?.` for safe calls, `?:` for a default, and smart casts after a null check.

`!!` throws a NullPointerException and should be rare. `lateinit` is for non-null properties set after construction (e.g. by DI); `by lazy` computes once on first access and is thread-safe by default.
points: Smart casts after checks (only on stable values)
lessons.tip: Platform types from Java are the hidden source of NPEs in Kotlin code. Mention annotating Java APIs with @Nullable/@NonNull.

code.title: lateinit vs lazy

lessons.title: Data, sealed and value classes
body: A **data class** generates `equals`, `hashCode`, `toString`, `copy` and `componentN` from the primary constructor. Only primary-constructor properties take part in equality.

A **sealed** class or interface restricts its subclasses to the same module and package, so `when` can be exhaustive with no `else`. That makes it perfect for UI state and results. A **value class** wraps one value with no allocation at runtime, giving type safety for IDs.
points: Sealed hierarchies for state and events
object for singletons, data object for sealed leaves
lessons.tip: When you add a new state, an exhaustive when turns a runtime bug into a compile error. Say exactly that in the interview.

code.title: Modelling screen state

lessons.title: Scope functions and extensions
body: `let`, `run`, `with`, `apply` and `also` differ in two ways: how they refer to the object (`it` or `this`) and what they return (the lambda result or the object itself).
Extension functions add functions to a type without inheritance. They are resolved **statically** from the declared type, so they cannot be overridden and cannot access private members.
points: apply: configure an object, returns it
let: transform or null-check, returns result
run / with: compute with this, returns result
lessons.tip: Overusing nested scope functions hurts readability. Interviewers like hearing "I keep them one level deep."

code.title: Choosing the right scope function
code.src:
val request = Request.Builder().apply {      // configure, returns the builder
    url(endpoint)
    header("Authorization", "Bearer $token")
}.build()

val user = repo.find(id)
    ?.also { log("found ${it.id}") }         // side effect, keeps the value
    ?.let { it.copy(name = it.name.trim()) } // transform

fun View.show(visible: Boolean) { isVisible = visible }   // extension

lessons.title: Higher-order functions, inline and generics
body: A lambda passed to a normal function is compiled to an object. `inline` copies the function body and the lambda into the call site, avoiding that allocation and allowing non-local `return`. Use `noinline` and `crossinline` when a lambda is stored or called from another context.
`reified` type parameters (only in inline functions) keep the type at runtime. Variance: `out T` means a producer (`List<out T>`), `in T` means a consumer (`Comparator<in T>`).
lessons.tip: Remember PECS from Java: Producer Extends, Consumer Super. In Kotlin that is out and in.

code.title: reified and variance in practice
code.src:
inline fun <reified T> Gson.fromJson(json: String): T =
    fromJson(json, object : TypeToken<T>() {}.type)

interface Source<out T> { fun next(): T }          // only produces T
interface Sink<in T> { fun put(item: T) }          // only consumes T

fun copy(from: Source<Number>, to: Sink<Int>) { /* ... */ }

val users: List<User> = gson.fromJson(json)        // no Class token needed

lessons.title: Introduction
body: In Compose you describe UI as a function of state: `UI = f(state)`. When state changes, Compose re-runs (**recomposes**) only the functions that read that state, and skips the rest when their inputs are unchanged.
Interview questions centre on three ideas: where state lives (hoisting), what triggers recomposition, and how to run side effects safely from a function that can run many times.
points: Composables are idempotent and side-effect free
Recomposition can be frequent, out of order, and skipped
State hoisting: state down, events up
lessons.tip: A stateless composable plus a thin stateful wrapper is the pattern interviewers want to see. It is easy to preview and test.

code.title: A stateless, hoisted composable

lessons.title: State, remember and hoisting
body: `mutableStateOf` creates observable state; `remember` keeps it across recompositions; `rememberSaveable` also keeps it across rotation and process death. Without `remember`, state resets on every recomposition.
Hoist state to the lowest common parent that needs it. Screen-level state belongs in a ViewModel exposed as `StateFlow`, collected with `collectAsStateWithLifecycle`.
points: derivedStateOf to limit recomposition from fast-changing state
Immutable state objects; avoid mutable collections in state
lessons.tip: Always pass key = { it.id } to lazy lists. It keeps item state stable when the list reorders, and interviewers notice when it is missing.

code.title: derivedStateOf for a scroll-dependent button

lessons.title: Recomposition and stability
body: Compose can **skip** a composable when all its parameters are stable and equal to last time. Primitive types, `String`, function types and classes annotated `@Immutable` or `@Stable` are stable; a `List` interface or a class with `var`s may not be.

Lambdas that capture unstable values, reading state too high in the tree, and creating new objects during composition all cause extra recompositions. Strong skipping mode (default in newer Compose compilers) relaxes some of these rules.
points: Read state as late as possible (lambda modifiers like offset { })
lessons.tip: Explain the three phases, composition → layout → drawing, and say a state read in a later phase skips the earlier ones.

code.title: Deferring a state read to the layout phase

lessons.title: Side effects
body: Composable functions must not perform side effects directly, because they can run any number of times. Use effect handlers. `LaunchedEffect(key)` runs a coroutine when it enters composition and restarts when the key changes. `DisposableEffect` adds cleanup. `SideEffect` publishes to non-Compose code after each successful recomposition.
`rememberCoroutineScope` gives a scope for event handlers like a button click. `rememberUpdatedState` lets a long-running effect see the latest value without restarting.
lessons.tip: LaunchedEffect(Unit) means "once per entering composition", not "once ever". It runs again after the composable leaves and comes back.

code.title: One-time events and lifecycle cleanup

lessons.title: Lists, navigation and performance
body: `LazyColumn` composes only visible items. Give items stable `key`s and a `contentType` so slots can be reused. Avoid heavy work inside item lambdas; precompute in the ViewModel.

For release performance, use **Baseline Profiles** (Compose is a library, so the first run is interpreted without them), keep R8 enabled, and always measure in a release build. Debug builds are much slower and give misleading results.
points: key and contentType in lazy lists
Precompute display strings in the ViewModel
lessons.tip: "I measured in a release build with a Baseline Profile" is the sentence that separates real Compose performance work from guesswork.

code.title: An efficient lazy list

lessons.title: Introduction
body: Coroutines are a **lightweight** way to write asynchronous code that reads like sequential code. A `suspend` function can pause without blocking its thread, so thousands of coroutines can share a few threads.
On Android you launch coroutines in a scope tied to a lifecycle, usually `viewModelScope` or `lifecycleScope`, so work is cancelled automatically when the screen goes away.
lessons.tip: Coroutines work great with lifecycle-aware components like ViewModel and lifecycleScope: cancellation comes for free.

code.title: Launching a coroutine

lessons.title: Coroutine basics
body: `launch` starts a coroutine that returns a `Job` and is used for fire-and-forget work. `async` returns a `Deferred<T>`, and you call `await()` for the result; use it to run independent work in parallel.

A `suspend` function can only be called from another suspend function or a coroutine. Suspending is cooperative: the function gives up its thread at suspension points such as `delay`, `withContext` or a network call written with suspend.
points: suspend means "can pause", not "runs in background"
runBlocking only in tests or main functions
lessons.tip: A suspend function does not switch threads by itself. Saying "suspend makes it run in the background" is a red flag in interviews.

code.title: Parallel calls with async

lessons.title: Coroutine scopes and dispatchers
body: A **scope** owns the coroutines started in it; cancelling the scope cancels all of them. A **dispatcher** decides which thread runs the code: `Main` for UI, `IO` for blocking I/O (a large, elastic pool), `Default` for CPU work (as many threads as cores).

Good practice is **main-safety**: every suspend function in your data layer switches to the right dispatcher itself with `withContext`, so callers can call it from Main. Inject dispatchers so tests can replace them.
lessons.tip: GlobalScope work is not tied to any lifecycle and leaks easily. If something must outlive a screen, use an application-level scope you control, or WorkManager.

code.title: Main-safe repository with an injected dispatcher

lessons.title: Structured concurrency and cancellation
body: Coroutines form a tree: a parent waits for its children, and cancelling a parent cancels its children. That is **structured concurrency**, and it prevents leaked work.

Cancellation is **cooperative**. Suspending functions from kotlinx check for it automatically, but a tight CPU loop must call `ensureActive()` or `yield()`. Never swallow `CancellationException` in a catch-all, or cancelled work keeps running.
lessons.tip: runCatching { } also catches CancellationException. Mention this subtle trap if the interviewer asks about error handling.

code.title: Cancellation-safe work

lessons.title: Error handling
body: An uncaught exception in a child of a regular `Job` cancels the parent and all siblings. With a `SupervisorJob` (or `supervisorScope`), a failing child does not affect its siblings. `viewModelScope` uses a SupervisorJob.

`launch` propagates exceptions to its parent immediately; `async` holds them until `await()`. A `CoroutineExceptionHandler` is a last resort for logging and only works on root coroutines, not to recover.
points: try/catch around the suspend call itself
lessons.tip: Classic question: "a SupervisorJob is the parent of two children and one throws. What happens?" Only that child fails; the sibling and parent continue.

code.title: Independent children with supervisorScope

lessons.title: Testing coroutines
body: Use `runTest` from kotlinx-coroutines-test. It skips `delay`s with virtual time so tests run instantly. Replace `Dispatchers.Main` with a test dispatcher via `Dispatchers.setMain` in a JUnit rule.
Pass a `StandardTestDispatcher` or `UnconfinedTestDispatcher` into classes that take a dispatcher, and use `advanceUntilIdle()` to run pending work.
lessons.tip: Injecting dispatchers is what makes this test possible. Tie testability back to the design decision.

code.title: A ViewModel test

articles.title: Best practices for coroutines in Android

lessons.title: Introduction
body: A `Flow` is an asynchronous stream of values. Most flows are **cold**: nothing runs until someone collects, and each collector gets its own run.
`StateFlow` and `SharedFlow` are **hot**: they exist independently of collectors. StateFlow always has a current value (great for UI state); SharedFlow broadcasts events to any number of subscribers.
lessons.tip: Explain cold vs hot with a cassette tape (each listener starts from the beginning) and a radio station (you hear whatever is on now).

code.title: A cold flow

lessons.title: Operators
body: Intermediate operators (`map`, `filter`, `onEach`, `debounce`, `distinctUntilChanged`) build a new flow and run nothing. Terminal operators (`collect`, `first`, `toList`, `launchIn`) start it.

The `flatMap` family differs in concurrency: `flatMapLatest` cancels the previous inner flow when a new value arrives (perfect for search), `flatMapConcat` runs them one after another, and `flatMapMerge` runs them concurrently. `combine` emits when either input changes; `zip` pairs values one-to-one.
lessons.tip: This one snippet answers half the Flow interview: debounce, flatMapLatest, error handling and stateIn.

code.title: Search-as-you-type

lessons.title: StateFlow and SharedFlow
body: `StateFlow` holds one value, needs an initial value, replays the latest value to new collectors, and **conflates**: equal consecutive values are dropped and slow collectors see only the latest. Use it for UI state.

`SharedFlow` is configurable (`replay`, `extraBufferCapacity`, `onBufferOverflow`) and has no current value. For one-off UI events, a `Channel` received as a flow guarantees each event is handled once, even while no one is collecting.
lessons.tip: WhileSubscribed(5000) keeps the upstream alive for 5 seconds, so a rotation does not restart the work. Explain why that number is used.

code.title: State plus one-off events in a ViewModel

lessons.title: Collecting safely on Android
body: Collecting in `lifecycleScope.launch { }` alone keeps collecting while the app is in the background, wasting resources and possibly crashing on UI updates. Use `repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED)` in Views, or `collectAsStateWithLifecycle()` in Compose.

`flowOn` changes the dispatcher of the **upstream** only; the collector keeps its own context. Never use `withContext` inside `flow { }` to emit from a different context; that breaks context preservation and throws.
lessons.tip: Forgetting awaitClose in callbackFlow leaks the listener. It is a favourite follow-up question.

code.title: Wrapping a callback API

lessons.title: Backpressure, errors and testing
body: Flows are sequential by default: the producer suspends until the collector finishes each value. `buffer()` runs producer and collector concurrently, `conflate()` drops intermediate values, and `collectLatest` cancels slow handling when a new value arrives.
`catch` handles upstream errors only; exceptions thrown in `collect` are not caught by it. Test flows with **Turbine**: `flow.test { assertEquals(x, awaitItem()) }`.
lessons.tip: Because StateFlow conflates, a fast Loading → Data change may skip Loading in tests. Know this before an interviewer asks why your test is flaky.

code.title: Testing a flow with Turbine

articles.title: Use Kotlin coroutines with lifecycle-aware components

lessons.title: Introduction
body: Good architecture keeps code easy to change and test. Android's recommended app architecture has a **UI layer** (screens and ViewModels), a **data layer** (repositories and data sources) and an optional **domain layer** (use cases).
Two rules make it work: **separation of concerns** (each class has one job) and **unidirectional data flow** (state flows down, events flow up).
points: UI layer, domain layer, data layer
lessons.tip: Start any architecture answer with the data flow, then the layers. Name the trade-off: more layers mean more files for small apps.

code.title: The layers in one flow

lessons.title: MVVM and the ViewModel
body: The ViewModel holds and exposes UI state, survives configuration changes and outlives the View. It must **never** hold a reference to a View, Activity or Fragment context, or it will leak them.
Expose one immutable state object (`StateFlow<ScreenUi>`) instead of many separate LiveData fields. That avoids inconsistent combinations, such as loading and error showing at the same time.
points: No Context or View references (use AndroidViewModel only if needed)
lessons.tip: If asked "MVVM vs MVP", say MVVM's ViewModel does not know the View, so it survives rotation and is easier to test.

code.title: A single UI state

lessons.title: MVI and unidirectional data flow
body: MVI models every user action as an **intent** (event), processes it with a reducer `(state, event) -> state`, and renders one immutable state. The flow is strictly one way, which makes behaviour predictable and easy to replay and debug.
The cost is boilerplate and the need to handle one-off effects (navigation, toasts) separately from state.
points: Pure reducers are easy to unit test
lessons.tip: Interviewers like a balanced view: MVI shines on complex screens with many interacting inputs, MVVM is enough for simple ones.

code.title: A minimal reducer

lessons.title: Repository, single source of truth and offline-first
body: A repository hides where data comes from. The usual pattern is that the **database is the single source of truth**: the UI observes Room, and the network only refreshes the database. That gives offline support and consistency for free.
Map network models (DTOs) and database entities to domain models at the boundary, so API changes do not ripple through the app.
points: Repository as the only entry point to data
Database as single source of truth
lessons.tip: Say "the UI never reads the network directly" when describing offline-first. It is the core idea in one line.

code.title: Offline-first repository

lessons.title: Clean Architecture and modularisation
body: Clean Architecture puts business rules in the centre (domain), with no Android dependencies, and frameworks at the edges. Dependencies point inward, and outer layers implement interfaces the inner layers define.

Splitting a large app into Gradle modules (`:core:data`, `:feature:checkout`) speeds up builds, enforces boundaries and lets teams work independently. Feature modules should depend on core modules, not on each other.
points: Use cases for reusable business logic
lessons.tip: Do not claim Clean Architecture is always right. Mention you would add a domain layer only when logic is shared or complex.

code.title: A typical module graph

lessons.title: Introduction
body: Dependency injection means a class receives its dependencies instead of creating them. That makes classes testable (pass a fake) and swappable (another implementation), and it centralises object lifetimes.
On Android the standard tool is **Hilt**, built on **Dagger**. Dagger generates the wiring code at compile time, so errors show up during the build instead of as crashes at runtime.
points: Compile-time graph (Dagger/Hilt) vs runtime service locator (Koin)
lessons.tip: Contrast Hilt (compile-time, safer, slower builds) with Koin (runtime, simpler, errors at runtime). A balanced answer scores better than a favourite.

code.title: Constructor injection

lessons.title: Hilt setup and components
body: Annotate the `Application` with `@HiltAndroidApp`, Android classes with `@AndroidEntryPoint`, and ViewModels with `@HiltViewModel`. Hilt provides a fixed hierarchy of **components**, each tied to an Android lifetime.

`SingletonComponent` lives as long as the app, `ActivityRetainedComponent` survives rotation, `ViewModelComponent` matches a ViewModel, and `ActivityComponent` and `FragmentComponent` match their owners. A child component can use bindings from its parents, not the other way round.
lessons.tip: Know that SavedStateHandle and @ApplicationContext are available without writing a module. Interviewers like that detail.

code.title: Wiring a ViewModel

lessons.title: Modules: @Provides and @Binds
body: Use a module when you cannot use constructor injection: interfaces, third-party classes (Retrofit, OkHttp, Room) or objects that need configuration.

`@Binds` maps an interface to its implementation and generates less code; it must be abstract. `@Provides` runs your code to build an instance. Put both kinds in separate modules, or put `@Provides` in a companion object.
lessons.tip: Why is @Binds better than @Provides for interfaces? It generates no factory method body, so builds are faster and the generated code smaller.

code.title: Network module

lessons.title: Scopes and qualifiers
body: Without a scope annotation, Hilt creates a **new instance every time** one is requested. A scope (`@Singleton`, `@ActivityRetainedScoped`, `@ViewModelScoped`) makes one instance per component. Scope only what must be shared or is expensive, because scoped objects stay in memory for the component's lifetime.
**Qualifiers** distinguish two bindings of the same type, for example two OkHttpClients or two dispatchers.
points: Scope annotation must match the component
lessons.tip: Over-scoping to @Singleton is a common mistake. Mention it as a memory concern when asked about scopes.

code.title: Qualifying dispatchers

lessons.title: Testing and assisted injection
body: In instrumented tests, annotate the test with `@HiltAndroidTest`, use `HiltAndroidRule`, and replace production modules with `@TestInstallIn`. For plain unit tests you usually do not need Hilt at all: call the constructor with fakes.
When an object needs both injected dependencies and a runtime value (an ID), use **assisted injection** with `@AssistedInject` and an `@AssistedFactory`.
points: Unit tests: just call the constructor
lessons.tip: Saying "my unit tests do not need Hilt because I use constructor injection" shows you understand why DI exists.

code.title: Assisted injection

lessons.title: Introduction
body: Most Android apps talk to a REST or GraphQL backend using **Retrofit** on top of **OkHttp**. Retrofit turns an annotated interface into HTTP calls; OkHttp does the actual work: connection pooling, HTTP/2, gzip, caching and interceptors.
Interviews test the full path: making calls main-safe, handling errors and timeouts, authentication with token refresh, caching, and security.
points: Retrofit builds requests, OkHttp executes them
lessons.tip: Share one OkHttpClient across the app (use newBuilder() for variants). Each client has its own connection pool and thread pool.

code.title: A Retrofit API

lessons.title: Interceptors
body: An interceptor sees every request and response. **Application interceptors** (`addInterceptor`) run once per call and see the final response. **Network interceptors** (`addNetworkInterceptor`) run for each network round-trip, including redirects, and see what goes on the wire.
Typical uses: adding auth and common headers, logging (debug builds only), request IDs, and rewriting cache headers.
lessons.tip: Never log Authorization headers or bodies in release builds. Mention redactHeader on the logging interceptor.

code.title: An auth header interceptor

lessons.title: Authentication and token refresh
body: When an access token expires, the server returns 401. OkHttp's **Authenticator** is called on a 401 and can return a new request with a refreshed token, or null to give up.
With many parallel requests, all of them can hit 401 at once. Synchronise the refresh so only one call refreshes and the others reuse the new token, and stop retrying after a limit to avoid loops.
points: Store tokens securely (EncryptedSharedPreferences or DataStore + Keystore)
lessons.tip: The "compare the token we sent with the current one" check is the detail that shows you have built this in production.

code.title: A single-flight token refresh

lessons.title: Errors, retries and caching
body: Model results explicitly: success, HTTP error (4xx/5xx with a body), network error (no connection, timeout) and unexpected errors. Retry only idempotent requests and transient failures, with exponential backoff and jitter.
OkHttp has an HTTP cache that honours `Cache-Control`. Give it a `Cache` directory and size, and let the server's headers decide freshness. For offline-first, cache in Room instead.
points: Typed results instead of throwing everywhere
Retry with backoff only for idempotent calls
lessons.tip: Mention exponential backoff with jitter: without jitter, all clients retry at the same moment and overload the server again.

code.title: A safe call wrapper

lessons.title: Security
body: All traffic should use HTTPS; Android blocks cleartext by default from API 28. A **network security config** controls trusted certificates, debug overrides and cleartext exceptions.

**Certificate pinning** (OkHttp `CertificatePinner`) defends against compromised CAs but can lock users out if certificates rotate, so pin backup keys and plan the rotation. Never put secrets in the APK; anything shipped can be extracted.
points: HTTPS only; cleartext blocked by default
No API secrets in the app; use a backend
lessons.tip: Always say "with a backup pin" when you mention pinning. Pinning a single key is how apps break on certificate rotation day.

code.title: Certificate pinning
code.src:
val pinner = CertificatePinner.Builder()
    .add("api.example.com", "sha256/AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA=")  // current key
    .add("api.example.com", "sha256/BBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBB=")  // backup key
    .build()

val client = OkHttpClient.Builder().certificatePinner(pinner).build()

lessons.title: Introduction
body: Android gives you several places to keep data: **Room** (SQLite) for structured, queryable data; **DataStore** for small key-value settings; files in app-specific storage for blobs; and MediaStore or the Storage Access Framework for shared files.
Picking the right one, keeping disk work off the main thread, and migrating schemas safely are the core interview themes.
points: All disk I/O off the main thread
lessons.tip: If asked "SharedPreferences vs DataStore", say: DataStore is async, uses Flow, handles errors and is safe from main-thread disk I/O.

code.title: Choosing storage

lessons.title: Room fundamentals
body: Room has three parts: `@Entity` (table), `@Dao` (queries) and `@Database` (holder). SQL queries are checked at **compile time**, which catches typos and missing columns before the app runs.
DAO methods can be `suspend` for one-shot work or return `Flow` to observe the table: Room re-emits whenever the tables used by the query change.
points: suspend for one-shot, Flow for observation
lessons.tip: Add indices for columns you filter or sort on. "How would you speed up this query?" usually wants an index.

code.title: Entity, DAO and an observable query

lessons.title: Migrations
body: Every schema change needs a database version bump and a migration. Without one, Room throws at startup, or wipes data if you used `fallbackToDestructiveMigration()`, which is rarely acceptable for user data.
Prefer **auto-migrations** for simple changes (adding a column or table), write a manual `Migration` for complex ones, and export schemas so you can test every path with `MigrationTestHelper`.
points: Bump version on every schema change
AutoMigration with specs for renames and deletes
lessons.tip: Mention testing migrations from every old version that users may still have, not only the previous one.

code.title: Auto and manual migrations

lessons.title: DataStore
body: **Preferences DataStore** stores key-value pairs; **Proto DataStore** stores a typed object defined by a schema. Both expose data as a `Flow` and write transactionally with `edit` or `updateData`.
Create one DataStore instance per file (use the `preferencesDataStore` delegate at top level). Two instances for the same file throw an exception.
points: Reads are Flow, writes are suspend
Not for large or relational data
lessons.tip: SharedPreferences.apply() still blocks the main thread during onPause in some cases. That is a concrete reason to move to DataStore.

code.title: Preferences DataStore

lessons.title: Offline-first and sync
body: In an offline-first app, the UI reads only from the local database; writes go to the database first and are synced to the server later. Track pending changes (a `syncState` column or an outbox table) and push them with **WorkManager** when there is a network connection.
Plan for conflicts: last-write-wins with server timestamps is simple; field-level merging or versions are safer when users edit the same data on several devices.
points: Local database is the source of truth
Paging 3 with RemoteMediator for large lists
lessons.tip: Use unique work so repeated triggers do not stack up duplicate syncs.

code.title: Queueing a sync with WorkManager

lessons.title: Introduction
body: Gradle turns source code and resources into an APK or App Bundle. The Android Gradle Plugin (AGP) adds Android tasks: resource merging, D8 dexing, R8 shrinking and signing.
Interviewers ask about build configuration (variants, flavours), dependency management, shrinking and obfuscation, and how to make builds faster in large projects.
lessons.tip: Explain compileSdk vs targetSdk vs minSdk in one line each. It is asked in almost every Android build question.

code.title: A minimal module build file

lessons.title: Build types and product flavours
body: **Build types** describe how you build (`debug`, `release`, maybe `benchmark`); **product flavours** describe what you build (`free`/`paid`, `dev`/`prod`). Gradle combines them into **build variants** such as `prodRelease`.
Each variant can have its own source set (`src/prod/`), resources, `BuildConfig` fields and application ID suffix, so dev and prod builds can be installed side by side.
lessons.tip: Never put real secrets in buildConfigField. They end up as plain strings in the APK.

code.title: Environments as flavours

lessons.title: Dependencies and version catalogs
body: `implementation` hides a dependency from modules that depend on yours, so changes do not force them to recompile. `api` exposes it. Prefer `implementation` for faster incremental builds.
A **version catalog** (`gradle/libs.versions.toml`) keeps all versions in one place with type-safe accessors. **BOMs** (Compose, Firebase, OkHttp) align versions across a library family.
lessons.tip: Explaining why implementation speeds up builds (smaller recompilation surface) shows you understand Gradle, not just its syntax.

code.title: A version catalog
code.src:
# gradle/libs.versions.toml
[versions]
kotlin = "2.0.21"
compose-bom = "2024.10.01"

[libraries]
compose-bom = { group = "androidx.compose", name = "compose-bom", version.ref = "compose-bom" }
compose-ui = { group = "androidx.compose.ui", name = "ui" }

[plugins]
kotlin-android = { id = "org.jetbrains.kotlin.android", version.ref = "kotlin" }

# build.gradle.kts
# implementation(platform(libs.compose.bom))
# implementation(libs.compose.ui)

lessons.title: R8: shrinking and obfuscation
body: In release builds, **R8** removes unused code (tree shaking), optimises and inlines it, and renames classes and members to short names. `isShrinkResources` also removes unused resources.

Code reached only by reflection (JSON models, some DI or serialization libraries) can be removed or renamed by mistake. Keep rules (`-keep`) tell R8 what to leave alone; many libraries ship their own consumer rules. Upload the `mapping.txt` file to deobfuscate crash stack traces.
points: Reflection is the usual cause of release-only crashes
lessons.tip: A crash that only happens in release is almost always R8 plus reflection. Say how you would find it: a minified debug build and the mapping file.

code.title: Release configuration

lessons.title: Faster builds
body: Large projects get slow builds from three things: configuration time, too much recompilation, and annotation processing. Fixes include the **configuration cache**, the **build cache**, modularisation with `implementation` dependencies, and **KSP** instead of kapt.
Measure before optimising: use a **build scan** or the Build Analyzer in Android Studio to see which tasks take the time.
points: Modularisation for parallel and incremental builds
lessons.tip: Quote a before and after ("clean build 6 min to 3 min") if you have one. Numbers make build answers credible.

code.title: gradle.properties for speed
code.src:
org.gradle.parallel=true
org.gradle.caching=true
org.gradle.configuration-cache=true
org.gradle.jvmargs=-Xmx4g -XX:+UseParallelGC
android.nonTransitiveRClass=true
kotlin.incremental=true

lessons.title: Introduction
body: Performance questions are about what the user feels: how fast the app starts, whether scrolling is smooth, whether it runs out of memory, and how much battery it uses.
The winning approach is always the same: **measure, find the bottleneck, fix it, measure again**, in a release build on a real low-end device.
lessons.tip: Interviewers distrust "it felt faster". Always say what you measured, with what tool, on which device.

code.title: Measuring startup with Macrobenchmark

lessons.title: App startup
body: **Cold** start creates the process, the Application and the first Activity; **warm** start reuses the process; **hot** start only brings the Activity to the front. Time to initial display (TTID) and time to full display (TTFD, reported with `reportFullyDrawn`) are the key metrics.

Common wins: move work out of `Application.onCreate`, initialise SDKs lazily or in the background, avoid disk and network on the main thread, and ship **Baseline Profiles** so hot code paths are compiled ahead of time.
points: Lazy SDK initialisation and App Startup library
lessons.tip: Baseline Profiles can improve startup and early interactions substantially, especially for Compose apps. Mention them in any startup answer.

code.title: Lazy initialisation instead of Application.onCreate

lessons.title: Rendering and jank
body: At 60 Hz each frame has about 16 ms; at 120 Hz about 8 ms. A frame that misses its deadline is **jank**. Causes include heavy work on the main thread, deep or over-measured layouts, overdraw, large bitmaps and garbage-collection pauses.

Find it with **Perfetto** / system traces, the JankStats library, and the Profileable release build. In RecyclerView, use `DiffUtil` / `ListAdapter`, stable IDs and fixed sizes; in Compose, avoid unnecessary recompositions.
lessons.tip: notifyDataSetChanged() redraws everything and kills animations. Saying you replaced it with ListAdapter is a quick, concrete win.

code.title: ListAdapter with DiffUtil

lessons.title: Memory and leaks
body: A leak happens when something long-lived (a singleton, a static field, a running coroutine or a listener) holds a reference to something short-lived, such as an Activity, View or Fragment. The garbage collector cannot free it.

Detect leaks with **LeakCanary** in debug builds and the Memory Profiler. Reduce memory pressure by sizing bitmaps to their view, using an image loader with caching (Coil or Glide), and responding to `onTrimMemory`.
points: Common leaks: static Context, listeners, inner classes, bindings
Avoid allocations in onDraw and hot loops
lessons.tip: When asked how you found a leak, describe the LeakCanary trace: the reference chain from a GC root to the leaked Activity.

code.title: A classic leak and its fix

lessons.title: Battery, network and app size
body: Batch and defer background work with WorkManager and constraints (charging, unmetered network). Avoid wake locks and frequent polling; use push messages (FCM) instead.

Network efficiency means fewer, smaller requests: compress responses, cache, paginate and prefetch only what is likely to be needed. App size affects install conversion; ship App Bundles, enable R8 and resource shrinking, and use WebP or vector images.
points: App Bundles and R8 for size
lessons.tip: Android vitals in the Play Console (ANR rate, crash rate, excessive wake-ups) is the production view interviewers expect a senior engineer to watch.

code.title: Deferring work to good conditions
code.src:
val upload = PeriodicWorkRequestBuilder<PhotoBackupWorker>(12, TimeUnit.HOURS)
    .setConstraints(
        Constraints(
            requiredNetworkType = NetworkType.UNMETERED,
            requiresCharging = true,
            requiresBatteryNotLow = true
        )
    )
    .build()
WorkManager.getInstance(ctx)
    .enqueueUniquePeriodicWork("photo-backup", ExistingPeriodicWorkPolicy.KEEP, upload)

lessons.title: Introduction
body: Behavioural rounds decide many offers, especially for senior roles. Interviewers want evidence of how you work: ownership, collaboration, handling conflict and failure, and the impact you had.
Prepare 6 to 8 real stories from your work and reuse them across questions. One story can show ownership, a technical decision and a lesson learned.
lessons.tip: Write your stories down before the interview. Under pressure, people forget their best examples.

code.title: A story bank template
code.src:
Story: Cut checkout crash rate
Situation : Checkout crashes at 1.8% after a payment SDK upgrade, peak sale in 2 weeks
Task      : I owned the fix as the payments module owner
Action    : Reproduced with a release build, found an R8 rule missing for SDK models,
            added a keep rule + a release smoke test in CI, coordinated with QA
Result    : Crash rate 1.8% -> 0.1%; no checkout incidents during the sale
Reuse for : ownership, debugging, working under pressure, process improvement

lessons.title: The STAR method
body: Structure each answer as **Situation**, **Task**, **Action**, **Result**. Spend most of the time on Action (what *you* did and why) and finish with a measurable Result and what you learned.
Keep answers to about two minutes. Let the interviewer ask follow-up questions instead of covering every detail up front.
points: Reflection: what you would do differently
lessons.tip: End with the result, not the action. Many candidates stop at "and then I shipped it".

code.title: A STAR answer in short form
code.src:
Q: Tell me about a time you improved performance.

S: Our feed scrolled at ~40 fps on low-end devices; reviews mentioned lag.
T: I was asked to fix it before the next release.
A: Profiled with Perfetto, found image decoding on the main thread and full
   list refreshes. Moved to Coil with sized requests and replaced
   notifyDataSetChanged with ListAdapter + DiffUtil. Added a Macrobenchmark.
R: Jank frames dropped from 18% to 3%; the benchmark now runs in CI.

lessons.title: Conflict, feedback and collaboration
body: Expect questions such as "tell me about a disagreement with a teammate or manager". Show that you disagreed on the problem, not the person, used data to decide, and committed to the outcome even when it was not your proposal.
For feedback questions, give a real example of feedback you received, what you changed, and how you know it worked.
points: Disagree on ideas with data, then commit
Show empathy for the other side
Working with product, design and backend
lessons.tip: Never make the other person the villain. Interviewers are checking whether you are someone they want on their team.

code.title: Structure for a disagreement answer
code.src:
1. The disagreement:  Compose rewrite now vs incremental migration
2. Their view:        Faster in the long run, cleaner code
3. My view:           Risk to the Q3 launch, team not yet trained
4. How we decided:    Built one screen both ways, measured effort and bugs
5. Outcome:           Incremental migration, new screens in Compose
6. What I learned:    Prototype early instead of arguing in meetings

lessons.title: Ownership, failure and leadership
body: A failure question tests self-awareness. Pick a real mistake with real consequences, own your part plainly, and spend most of the answer on what you changed afterwards: a process, a test, a habit.
Senior roles add leadership without authority: mentoring, driving a technical decision across teams, improving engineering practices, and making trade-offs between speed and quality.
lessons.tip: Avoid fake failures like "I work too hard". They signal a lack of self-awareness.

code.title: Turning a failure into a strong answer
code.src:
Mistake : Shipped a migration that wiped local drafts for ~2% of users
Owned   : I wrote the migration and skipped testing from an older schema
Fixed   : Hotfix within 6 hours, restored drafts from server copies
Changed : Added MigrationTestHelper tests for every historic version,
          added a staged rollout rule for DB changes
Lesson  : Test the upgrade paths users actually have, not just the latest

lessons.title: Questions to ask and closing
body: At the end you will be asked whether you have questions. Ask about the team's real problems: how they ship, how they measure quality, what the first 90 days look like, and what success means in this role.
Use your last minute to connect your experience to their needs in one or two sentences.
points: Ask about the team, product and engineering practices
Ask what success looks like in 3 to 6 months
Avoid salary questions in technical rounds
Close with a short fit summary
lessons.tip: Questions about their release process and quality metrics show you think like an owner, not only an implementer.

code.title: Good questions to ask
code.src:
- What does a typical release look like, from PR to Play Store rollout?
- How do you measure app quality today (crash rate, ANRs, performance)?
- What is the biggest technical challenge the Android team faces this year?
- What would make someone very successful in this role in six months?
- How are architecture decisions made and documented?

lessons.title: Introduction
body: Mobile system design asks you to design an app or SDK end to end in 45 to 60 minutes: requirements, architecture, data flow, offline behaviour, APIs and trade-offs. There is no single right answer; interviewers grade your reasoning and communication.
Mobile rounds differ from backend ones: they focus on the client (caching, sync, battery, flaky networks, app size and lifecycle), with the backend treated mostly as an API.
lessons.tip: Say the time plan out loud at the start. It shows structure and lets the interviewer steer you to what they care about.

code.title: A 45-minute plan
code.src:
0-5 min   Clarify: features in scope, users, scale, offline needs, platforms
5-15 min  High-level design: screens, modules, layers, data flow diagram
15-30 min Deep dive: data model, API, caching, pagination, sync, errors
30-40 min Non-functional: performance, battery, security, testing, monitoring
40-45 min Trade-offs, what you would do next, questions

lessons.title: Requirements and API design
body: Split requirements into **functional** (what the app does) and **non-functional** (latency, offline, battery, security, scale). Confirm scope before designing; it is fine to say which features you will leave out.
Design the API contract the app needs: endpoints or GraphQL queries, cursor-based pagination, error formats, and whether to use polling, push notifications, SSE or WebSockets for real-time updates.
lessons.tip: Cursor pagination does not skip or duplicate items when new posts arrive. Explain why offset pagination fails for feeds.

code.title: A feed API contract
code.src:
GET /v1/feed?cursor=eyJpZCI6...&limit=20
200 {
  "items": [{ "id": "p_91", "author": {...}, "media": [...], "createdAt": 1729420000 }],
  "nextCursor": "eyJpZCI6InBfNzIifQ",
  "hasMore": true
}

POST /v1/posts/p_91/like
Idempotency-Key: 7f9c-...      # safe to retry on flaky networks

lessons.title: Client architecture
body: Describe the layers: UI (Compose screens + ViewModels), domain (optional use cases) and data (repositories over a local database and the network). The database is the single source of truth and the UI observes it.
Name the key components: image loader, pagination (Paging 3 with RemoteMediator), background sync (WorkManager), push (FCM), analytics and a feature-flag layer.
lessons.tip: Draw the arrow API → database → UI, never API → UI. It is the one diagram every mobile design answer should have.

code.title: Data flow for a paged feed

lessons.title: Offline, sync and real time
body: Decide what must work offline: reading cached content, composing actions (likes, messages) that are queued and sent later. Store pending actions in an outbox table and send them with WorkManager, using idempotency keys so retries are safe.
For real-time features (chat, live location), use a WebSocket while the app is in the foreground, FCM to wake the app for important events, and a sync-on-open fallback to catch up on anything missed.
points: WebSocket in foreground, FCM in background
Catch-up sync with a last-seen cursor
lessons.tip: Mention what happens when the server rejects a queued action. Interviewers often probe the unhappy path.

code.title: Optimistic like with an outbox

lessons.title: Non-functional concerns and trade-offs
body: Cover performance (startup, scroll, image sizes), battery (batching, constraints), security (token storage, pinning, no secrets in the app), observability (crash reporting, analytics, performance monitoring) and rollout (feature flags, staged releases).
Close by naming trade-offs explicitly: what you chose, what you gave up and when you would choose differently. That is what separates senior answers.
lessons.tip: Practise with Droidly's system design walkthroughs below. Do each one out loud with a timer.

code.title: Stating a trade-off clearly
code.src:
Decision : WebSocket for chat while the app is open
Gain     : Sub-second delivery, typing indicators
Cost     : Battery and connection handling; must reconnect with backoff
Fallback : FCM data messages when backgrounded + sync on open
Revisit  : If most users are on poor networks, consider long polling
